# **Abstract** 

Human vision integrates multiple features into a coherent perception of an object or scene, yet the mechanisms underlying this binding process remain only partially understood. Color–motion misbinding, a phenomenon in which peripheral stimuli are systematically misperceived as carrying the color–motion pairing of a simultaneously presented central stimulus, offers a window into these mechanisms. Zhang et al. (2014) reported that such misbinding induces a color-contingent motion aftereffect (misbinding-induced CCMAE), implying that illusory feature conjunctions are registered at a cortical stage capable of driving sensory adaptation. 🔴We tested this claim in two experiments differing in the range of test speeds. 🔴Psychometric functions were fitted to observers' directional judgments, and Bayesian paired comparisons assessed differences in the point of subjective equality (PSE) and slope between misbinding and control conditions. 🔴Neither experiment provided credible evidence for a PSE shift, a conclusion that was robust to participant exclusion, to the choice of Bayes-factor prior, and to a supplementary trial-level hierarchical model. 🔴🔴In one experiment, the psychometric slope was shallower in the misbinding than the control condition. 🔴The absence of a reliable shift in PSE indicates that the color–motion misbinding aftereffect is more fragile than previously assumed. Instead, motion-direction sensitivity was reduced in the misbinding condition. These results may reflect a misbinding-induced CCMAE that is genuine but weak, or they may indicate that misbinding arises from a higher-level perceptual inference that does not strongly modulate the motion-selective neurons driving directional aftereffects.

# **Keywords** 

feature binding, visual illusion, motion, color, aftereffect, peripheral vision

# **Introduction**

Human vision seamlessly integrates multiple features—such as color, shape, and motion—into the coherent perception of objects. A red ball rolling across the floor is perceived as a single entity, not as separate impressions of redness, roundness, and movement. However, neurophysiological evidence has traditionally suggested a degree of functional specialization for different visual features, such as color and motion, in early visual processing [(Livingstone & Hubel, 1988; Zeki, 1978](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/dXRN+VIt4); but see [Seymour et al., 2009\)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/RoM0) . This raises the classic "binding problem": how does the brain reassemble these features into a unified percept? [(Holcombe & Cavanagh, 2001; Seymour et al., 2009; Wolfe & Cave, 1999](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/ln2H+RoM0+VPyd); but see [Di Lollo, 2012\)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/PDBd). 

Feature Integration Theory [(Treisman & Gelade, 1980\)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/jPex) offers a classical answer. On this account, basic features such as color and orientation are registered preattentively, and focused attention is what binds them into correct combinations. When attention is absent or insufficient, features can combine incorrectly [(Treisman & Schmidt, 1982\)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/sgxr). 

An example of such misbinding was reported by [Wu et al. (2004)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/KO08). Observers fixated centrally while two transparent surfaces of random dots moved in opposite directions (e.g., upward-moving green dots and downward-moving red dots). In the periphery, the colors were physically swapped (upward red, downward green), yet observers reported seeing the central pairing extend continuously across the entire display (see the **Supplementary movie;** also available at https://youtu.be/Nv4RYz4O0K0). 

Wu et al.'s illusion has gained considerable interest [(Crayen et al., 2024; Gunther & McKinney, 2020; Stepien & Shevell, 2015; Suzuki et al., 2013; Wang & Shevell, 2014; Zhang et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2016, 2019\)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/mO3P+VArW+EneI+eujU+zthm+Ky43+36Hc+U28A), in part because it “solidifies the evidence for the existence of a binding problem” [(Wu et al., 2004\)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/KO08). Unlike classical illusory conjunctions, which are brief and spatially restricted [(Treisman, 1998; Treisman & Schmidt, 1982\)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/sgxr+LJuE), this illusion is robust both in space and in time, making it a useful tool for probing the neural basis of feature binding. Building on this property, previous studies [(Zhang et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2016\)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/U28A+Ky43) asked whether motion aftereffects could be contingent on the illusory color–motion pairing of this illusion. They found that, after adapting to a misbinding display, observers showed motion aftereffects consistent with the illusory rather than the physical pairing. This is rare evidence that an illusory feature conjunction can be represented at a stage of processing capable of driving feature-contingent adaptation.

Recent work on peripheral vision, however, suggests a different reading of Wu et al.'s illusion. Studies of visual crowding indicate that peripheral perception is constrained not only by reduced spatial resolution and attentional limits, but also by pooling and averaging, which increase uncertainty about which features belong to which places or objects [(Balas et al., 2009; Harrison & Bex, 2017; Pelli et al., 2004; Rosenholtz, 2016, 2025; Schwetlick & Herzog, 2025; Whitney & Levi, 2011\)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/86rf+lx2j+Pocq+rYAd+SiO9+yuhO+iUbx). On this view, peripheral vision deals in ensembles and summary statistics rather than in discrete, individuated features. Wu et al.‘s illusion, which arises more frequently in the periphery than at the fovea [(Bi et al., 2022\)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/qxEK), may thus reflect the inherently cluttered character of peripheral encoding. If the features that binding would unite do not exist as separable entities to begin with, it is not so obvious that adaptation to a "misbound" percept should produce a strong feature-contingent aftereffect at all. Indeed, the aftereffects reported for summary statistics are confined to a single dimension [(Corbett et al., 2012\)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/QuZ9), and no study has shown adaptation to a feature conjunction defined over an ensemble of items. 

Against this background, the misbinding-induced CCMAE reported by Zhang et al. (2014) takes on particular significance. If illusory feature conjunctions can drive a color-contingent aftereffect, this would imply that they are registered at a cortical stage capable of sensory adaptation. Whether this aftereffect is robust bears directly on how misbinding should be understood. 🔴The present study therefore tested this claim in two experiments: Experiment 1 closely followed the test speeds used by Zhang et al. (2014), and Experiment 2 extended testing to slower speeds that had not previously been examined. 🔴🔴Unlike Zhang et al. (2014), who counterbalanced the color–motion pairing of the adaptor across participants, we fixed this pairing within each adaptation condition to simplify the design (see Methods). 🔴🔴This is a departure from a fully direct replication of the original study, and we return to its implications throughout the Results and Discussion.🔴

# **Methods**

This study was preregistered: [https://osf.io/fnruy](https://osf.io/fnruy). The data and analysis scripts are available: [https://github.com/LNOKB/Misbinding/tree/main/CCMAE\_exp1](https://github.com/LNOKB/Misbinding/tree/main/CCMAE_exp1). The research protocol for this project was reviewed and approved by the Research Ethics Committee of the Graduate School of Informatics at Kyoto University under the reference number KUIS-EAR-2024-003. The method of this experiment was identical to that used in Experiment 1 of [Zhang et al. (2014)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/U28A), except that the color–motion pairing was fixed for simplification.

## Participants 

🔴[Zhang et al. (2014)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/U28A) report only significance levels (*p*-values) for the relevant comparisons, not an effect size or the descriptive statistics needed to compute one, so an a priori power analysis based on their effect size was not possible; we therefore recruited twelve participants, matching their sample size instead. 🔴All participants were recruited via Kyoto University's system. They were naïve to the purpose of the study and screened with the Ishihara test. They gave written informed consent before participation. 

## Apparatus

Stimuli were displayed on an LCD monitor, a 24-inch EIZO EV2451. The monitor was set to a spatial resolution of 1024 × 768 pixels and a refresh rate of 60 Hz. Psychtoolbox extensions [(Brainard, 1997\)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/9bmc) were used for stimulus display and data collection in Matlab. Participants sat 57 cm away from the screen, using a chin rest to stabilize the head position. Luminance and chromaticity were measured with a luminance colorimeter, KONICA MINOLTA, CS-150. 

## Stimuli 

The experiment employed a fully crossed 2 × 2 × 5 within-subjects design, with adaptation condition (misbinding vs. control), test stimulus color (red vs. green), and test stimulus speed (0.6°/sec upward, 0.3°/sec upward, 0°/sec, 0.3°/sec downward, 0.6°/sec downward) as factors. Adaptation screens (20° width ×14° height) contained two sheets of random dots, one sheet moving up and the other moving down. The colors of the dots were either red (x=0.637, y=0.349, 18.9 cd/m2) or green (x=0.334, y=0.535, 18.2 cd/m2). Dot diameters were 0.1°, speeds were 3°/sec, and density was 8 dots per deg2. 

In the misbinding condition, the left and middle sides of the adaptation screens (“induction part”; 16°×14°) and the remaining right peripheral area (“effect part”; 4°×14°) were rendered with opposite color–motion pairing. We expected that this would induce the color–motion misbinding in the effect part. In the control condition, nothing was presented in the effect area. The previous study [(Zhang et al., 2014\)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/U28A) counterbalanced the combination of color–motion pairing (red-up and green-down vs. red-down and green-up) and adaptation condition (misbinding vs. control). However, they found similar results across these combinations and pooled the results for the analysis. Therefore, we used a single color–motion pairing for each adaptation condition (**Table 1**).

|  | Induction part stimuli | Effect part stimuli |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Misbinding condition** | red-up, green-down | red-down, green-up |
| **Control condition** | red-down, green-up | — |

**Table 1\. Physical color–motion pairings in the adaptation stimuli.** In the misbinding condition, the induction part contained red dots moving upward and green dots moving downward, whereas the effect part contained the opposite physical color–motion pairings. This configuration is expected to induce the perceptual misbinding of color and motion, such that the effect part is perceived as sharing the same color–motion pairings as the induction part. In the control condition, only the induction part was presented during adaptation, and no effect-part stimulus was shown.

There were 10 types of test stimuli. They were red or green dots presented in the effect part (**Figure 1**), with one of five different speeds (0.6°/sec upward, 0.3°/sec upward, 0°/sec, 0.3°/sec downward, 0.6°/sec downward). 

## Procedure 

Participants performed the experiment in a dark room. Throughout the experiments, a white cross was presented at the center of the screen, and participants were asked to fixate on it, except when pressing a key. Eye movements were not recorded because the perception of misbinding was not confined to a small, fixed region but was distributed across the entire display [(Wu et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2014\)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/KO08+U28A), likely limiting the impact of fixation fluctuations. 🔴However, because the test stimulus itself was brief (0.2 s) and confined to a narrow peripheral strip, small eye movements could still have altered its retinal eccentricity or displaced it toward the adapted or unadapted region; we did not verify fixation stability directly, and we treat this as an open limitation, particularly for interpreting the null PSE results (see Discussion). 🔴The experiment consisted of 20 blocks of 40 trials, 10 blocks for each adaptation condition (misbinding vs. control). 🔴The order of the 20 blocks was independently randomized for each participant, minimizing the confounding of adaptation condition with fatigue or learning effects. 🔴Each block began with a 30-sec pre-adaptation, followed by the 40 trials (**Figure 1**). The pre-adaptation display was the same as the adaptation display used in each trial, except for its duration. In a trial, after a 5-sec adaptation and a 0.2-sec blank interval, test stimuli were presented for 0.2 sec, and participants were asked to make a 2-AFC judgment on the motion direction of the test stimulus, either upward or downward (**Figure 1**).   
![][image1]  
**Figure 1\. Trial time course.** After a 5-sec adaptation and a 0.2-sec blank interval, test stimuli were presented for 0.2 sec. The gray dashed line in the adaptation and test screen shows the border between the induction and effect parts. This boundary was not visible during the experiment and is shown for illustrative purposes only. In the misbinding condition, the induction part and the effect part were rendered with opposite color–motion pairing. In the control condition, nothing was presented on the effect part. Test stimuli were either red or green and moved at one of five speeds (0.6°/sec upward, 0.3°/sec upward, 0°/sec, 0.3°/sec downward, 0.6°/sec downward).  Participants were asked to make a 2-AFC judgment on the motion direction of the test stimulus, indicating whether the test stimulus appeared to move upward or downward.

## Data Analysis 

We pooled the data regarding test stimuli color and plotted the percentage of trials in which participants indicated directions for the test stimuli that were opposite to the moving direction of inducer part dots, as a function of the speed of the test stimulus (**Figure 2**). Individual participant results before and after this pooling are shown in **Supplementary Figures 1 and 2**, respectively. This value reflects the extent to which perception of the test stimulus was biased by the perceived color–motion misbinding, in a manner consistent with a motion aftereffect (i.e., a repulsive shift away from the adapting direction). 

![][image2]  
**Figure 2\. Data analysis pipeline.** The left panels show the data for the red (top) and green (bottom) test stimuli. In the misbinding condition, the dots in the induction part  
moved upward when red and downward when green (see **Table 1**). Assuming that the effect part is perceived as having the same color–motion pairing as this inducer part, and the visual system adapts to this illusory combination, red/green test dots were predicted to appear to move downward / upward, respectively. Therefore, we showed the “downward” / “upward” response rate for red/green test dots, respectively, in the left panels. Following the previous study [(Zhang et al., 2014\)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/U28A), these data were pooled together for analysis (right panel). The x-axis of the right panel represents the speed and relative direction of the test stimulus. S and O indicate whether the test stimulus moved in the same or opposite direction, respectively, relative to the physical motion direction of the inducer part dots with the same color. For example, if the green test dots moved upward at 0.6°/s in the misbinding condition, this condition was labeled the "O0.6" condition. The y-axis shows the percentage of trials in which observers judged the test stimulus as moving in the opposite direction to the physical motion of the inducer part dots. This value refers to the amount of motion aftereffect contingent on misbound color.

We fitted psychometric functions for pooled data (**Figure 2**). For each participant and condition (misbinding vs. control), responses were fitted with a logistic function:  
[![][image3]](https://www.codecogs.com/eqnedit.php?latex=%5Cfrac%7B1%7D%7B1%2B%5Cexp\(-%5Cbeta\(x-%5Calpha\)\)%7D#0)  
where α represents the point of subjective equality (PSE), and β represents the slope parameter. Higher values of α indicate a larger shift of the psychometric function along the x-axis, whereas larger values of β indicate steeper psychometric functions.  🔴Fitting was performed using the quickpsy package for R [(Linares & López-Moliner, 2016\)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/sQzn). 🔴🔴Lapse and guessing rates were not estimated freely for each participant because, with only five speed levels per psychometric function, per-participant estimates of a four-parameter logistic function are unstable. 🔴🔴The lapse rate was fixed at 0.03, a value within the conventional 1%–5% range used in the psychophysics literature (Wichmann & Hill, 2001). 🔴🔴Because the dependent variable was the tendency of observers to judge the test stimulus as moving in the opposite direction to the physical motion of the inducer part dots, rather than the accuracy of a forced-choice discrimination, we assumed the guessing rate to be at the same level as the lapse rate and likewise fixed it at 0.03.🔴

Following the previous study ([Zhang et al., 2014\)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/U28A), PSE served as the primary measure of the misbinding-induced CCMAE. A leftward shift of the psychometric function in the misbinding condition relative to the control condition would indicate a bias in perceived motion direction induced by adaptation to the illusory color–motion pairing, showing the presence of a misbinding-induced CCMAE.

Participants whose responses showed little systematic dependence on test speed were excluded from the analyses due to unreliable task performance. 🔴Based on this criterion, two participants' data were excluded from Experiment 1, and (as described in the Results) five participants' data were excluded from Experiment 2. 🔴🔴Because this criterion was not preregistered, we report the corresponding analyses of the complete, unexcluded samples alongside the excluded-sample analyses throughout the Results. 🔴**Supplementary Figures 1 and 2** show the data of all participants. 

# **Results**

## Results of Experiment 1

Following the previous studies [(Zhang et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2016\)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/U28A+Ky43), we hypothesized that the psychometric function in the misbinding condition would be shifted leftward relative to that in the control condition, indicating the presence of a misbinding-induced CCMAE. 

**Figure 3a** shows the psychometric functions for the misbinding (red) and control (blue) conditions, together with their estimated PSE and slope parameters (**Figure 3b, 3c**). Following the preregistered analysis plan and the previous study’s method [(Zhang et al., 2014\)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/U28A), the participant-wise PSE differences between the misbinding and control conditions were submitted to a one-sample t-test against zero, and the same test was applied to the slope differences as a non-preregistered supplementary check. 🔴Neither test showed a significant difference (PSE: *t*(9) \= –0.65, *p* \= .534, mean difference \= –0.024, 95% CI [–0.107, 0.060], *Cohen’s d* \= –0.20; slope: *t*(9) \= –0.09, *p* \= .933, mean difference \= –0.045, 95% CI [–1.205, 1.116], *Cohen’s d* \= –0.03). 🔴Because these non-significant frequentist tests alone do not provide direct evidence for the absence of an effect, we conducted a complementary Bayesian analysis to quantify the evidence for or against a non-zero difference. A Bayesian paired t-test was conducted to compare the PSE and slope of these psychometric functions between the misbinding and control conditions, using the BayesFactor package in R [(Morey & Rouder, 2024\)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/8qZo) with a default Cauchy prior (r \= 1/√2). The Bayes factor (BF₁₀) quantifies the evidence in favor of the alternative hypothesis (H₁: a difference exists between conditions) relative to the null hypothesis (H₀: no difference). 🔴These analyses provided evidence favoring the null hypothesis, with Bayes Factors (BF₁₀) of 0.37 for PSE and 0.31 for slope. 🔴Contrary to the findings of the previous study [(Zhang et al., 2014\)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/U28A), misbinding did not induce a credible shift in PSE. 

🔴This pattern of results was robust across several checks reported in full in the **Supplementary Material**. It held when all twelve participants were included without exclusion (BF₁₀ \= 0.34 for PSE, 0.29 for slope), and its qualitative conclusion did not depend on the width of the Bayes-factor prior (PSE: BF₁₀ range 0.21–0.70; slope: BF₁₀ range 0.17–0.64, across four prior widths spanning the range conventionally used in the literature; **Supplementary Table 1**). On the other hand, the Bayes-factor analysis was not preregistered, so the design of this experiment, such as sample size, was not optimized for this analysis. As a result, a design-sensitivity analysis, simulating our design under conventional small, medium, and large true effect sizes (**Supplementary Table 1**), shows that detection rates were low throughout, indicating limited sensitivity to a small-to-moderate misbinding-induced CCMAE. The present null result is therefore better read as inconclusive with respect to such an effect than as positive evidence of its absence. In addition, we also built a supplementary hierarchical logistic mixed-effects model, which fits directly to the raw trial-level responses (`lme4::glmer`; Bates et al., 2015), rather than to the two-stage per-participant point estimates used above. Likewise, it showed no credible condition effect on either the PSE-shift or slope-difference terms (excluded sample: both |*z*| \< 0.71, both *p* \> .48; all participants: both |*z*| \< 0.60, both *p* \> .55; **Supplementary Table 2**).🔴

One possible explanation is that the test speeds adopted from the previous study [(Zhang et al., 2014\)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/U28A) were not optimal for the present sample. Because motion sensitivity varies substantially across individuals, the test speeds used in Experiment 1 may have reduced sensitivity to subtle perceptual biases induced by the illusion. To address this possibility, Experiment 2 employed slower test speeds in an attempt to increase sensitivity to any adaptation effects arising from color–motion misbinding.

## Results of Experiment 2

To address the possibility that the relatively high test speeds used in Experiment 1 reduced sensitivity to subtle perceptual biases, Experiment 2 employed slower test stimuli. The method was identical to that of Experiment 1, except that the test stimulus could move at one of five speeds: 0.4°/s upward, 0.2°/s upward, 0°/s, 0.2°/s downward, or 0.4°/s downward. Experiment 2 used the same design and analysis as the preregistered Experiment 1, differing only in the test speeds, and was not independently preregistered. Twelve participants were recruited, matching the sample size of Experiment 1\. None of the participants had taken part in Experiment 1\. Based on the data exclusion criteria, five participants' data were excluded from subsequent analysis. All participant results before and after pooling are shown in **Supplementary Figures 3 and 4**, respectively. The data and analysis scripts for Experiment 2 are available: [https://github.com/LNOKB/Misbinding/tree/main/CCMAE\_exp2](https://github.com/LNOKB/Misbinding/tree/main/CCMAE_exp1). 

**Figure 4a** shows the psychometric functions for the misbinding (red) and control (blue) conditions, together with their estimated PSE and slope parameters (**Figure 4b, 4c**). As in Experiment 1, the participant-wise PSE differences between the misbinding and control conditions were submitted to a one-sample t-test against zero, and the same test was applied to the slope differences as a non-preregistered supplementary check. 🔴Neither test showed a significant difference (PSE: *t*(6) \= 0.77, *p* \= .469, mean difference \= 0.022, 95% CI [–0.047, 0.090], *Cohen’s d* \= 0.29; slope: *t*(6) \= –2.37, *p* \= .055, mean difference \= –4.81, 95% CI [–9.78, 0.15], *Cohen’s d* \= –0.90). 🔴🔴A Bayesian paired-samples t-test provided anecdotal evidence in favor of the null hypothesis for PSE (BF₁₀ \= 0.45; **Figure 4b**), consistent with Experiment 1 and indicating no reliable PSE shift. 🔴🔴As in Experiment 1, this null PSE result was robust to including all twelve participants without exclusion (BF₁₀ \= 0.52), to prior width (BF₁₀ range 0.27–0.77; **Supplementary Table 1**), to a supplementary hierarchical trial-level model (excluded sample: |*z*| \= 0.17, *p* \= .87; all participants: |*z*| \= 0.28, *p* \= .78; **Supplementary Table 2**).🔴

🔴For the slope of the psychometric function, a different pattern was suggested, though the evidence was not strong: the control condition produced steeper functions than the misbinding condition, but only with anecdotal evidence (BF₁₀ \= 1.84; **Figure 4c**). 🔴🔴This evidence remained anecdotal-to-moderate across prior widths (BF₁₀ range 1.51–1.84; **Supplementary Table 1**) and was similarly inconclusive in the complete, unexcluded sample (BF₁₀ \= 0.85). 🔴🔴A supplementary analysis of the two test colors separately is reported with Supplementary Figure 3.🔴

🔴The results of Experiments 1 and 2 provide no credible evidence for a PSE shift attributable to a misbinding-induced CCMAE when test colors are pooled, though a supplementary analysis of Experiment 1 that considered the two test colors separately (Supplementary Figure 1) suggests that this pooled null result should not be over-interpreted as ruling out any color-specific bias. Unlike the previous study (Zhang et al., 2014), we did not counterbalance the color–motion pairing across the misbinding and control conditions, which may have reduced our sensitivity to the misbinding-induced CCMAE. This is a genuine limitation of the present design that a counterbalanced replication would be needed to resolve. In addition, the Experiment 2 slope result suggests that adaptation to color–motion misbinding influences the precision of motion-direction judgments even when it does not systematically bias the judgment itself. We discuss several possible explanations for these results, and the design confounds that limit their interpretation, in the **Discussion** section.🔴

![][image5]  
**Figure 4\. Results of Experiment 2 (a)** Psychometric functions and the corresponding estimates of **(b)** PSE and **(c)** slope in Experiment 2\. The format of this figure is identical to that of Figure 3\.

# **Discussion**

The present study sought to replicate and extend the findings of [Zhang et al. (2014) and Zhang et al. (2016)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/U28A+Ky43), who reported that adaptation to illusory color–motion misbinding in peripheral vision produced a measurable shift in PSE for subsequent motion-direction judgments. 🔴Across two experiments, one using the original test speeds and the other extending testing to slower speeds, we found no credible evidence of a PSE shift in either experiment, and this null result was robust to participant exclusion, to Bayes-factor prior width, and to a supplementary hierarchical trial-level model (see Results). 🔴🔴In Experiment 2, we also observed a shallower psychometric slope in the misbinding than the control condition though it remains anecdotal evidence. 🔴🔴In the following sections, we discuss several possible explanations for the absence of a PSE shift and for the reduced sensitivity in the misbinding condition.🔴

🔴There are two broad possibilities. First, a misbinding-induced CCMAE may have been present, but our experimental design failed to detect it. Second, a misbinding-induced CCMAE may not exist, or may be substantially weaker than previously assumed, under the conditions tested here.🔴

🔴Several aspects of the present design depart from the original study in ways that could have limited our ability to detect a true effect. The color–motion pairing of the adaptor was not counterbalanced across participants (see Introduction), and eye movements were not recorded, so we cannot rule out that fixation instability altered the retinal eccentricity of the brief (0.2 s), spatially restricted test stimulus in a way that differed between conditions. For these reasons, we cannot rule out the possibility that a misbinding-induced CCMAE was present in our data but went undetected.🔴

🔴A related possibility is that a misbinding-induced CCMAE was present but partially cancelled by an ordinary, veridical CCMAE. In the misbinding display used in the present study (see **Figure 1**), the direction of adaptation from the veridical stimulus and the illusory pairing perceived by the observer are in opposition. If misbinding operates in the same manner as veridical binding, a single color would be bound to two motion signals of opposite direction: one corresponding to the veridical pairing and the other to the illusory pairing. Adaptation driven by the veridical stimulus and adaptation driven by the illusory percept may then have partially cancelled each other; because the color in the effect part is bound to two opposing motion directions, adaptation may have been distributed across both, broadening the psychometric function. Such a pattern, a shallower slope without a systematic change in the PSE, is consistent with the exploratory Experiment 2 slope result described above, although we did not observe it in Experiment 1. If this cancellation account is correct, it should in principle also have applied in Zhang et al. (2014), whose adaptation configuration was materially similar to ours; yet this account cannot explain why they nonetheless reported a reliable PSE shift, since the same cancellation should have suppressed it there as well. We cannot check whether a corresponding slope pattern was also present in their data, because Zhang et al. (2014) did not report slope estimates. One candidate disanalogy is that Zhang et al. (2014) counterbalanced the color–motion pairing across participants, whereas the present study fixed it for simplification (see Introduction and Methods), which could have made a constant, non-cancelling bias more visible in our design.🔴

🔴That said, the slope effect itself admits other explanations. In particular, our control condition may not cleanly isolate misbinding from ordinary sensory adaptation: because the effect part was physically stimulated throughout adaptation in the misbinding condition but left entirely unstimulated in the control condition, a shallower slope could equally reflect ordinary local motion adaptation or masking rather than misbinding-induced adaptation specifically (see Methods).🔴

🔴Turning to the second possibility, one reason a misbinding-induced CCMAE might be weak or absent is that aftereffects induced by illusory stimuli are generally weaker than those produced by real physical stimuli [(Huk et al., 2001; van Lier et al., 2009; Winawer et al., 2008\)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/xbek+nBuh+1RR8). Supplementary data from [Zhang et al. (2014)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/U28A) show that a correctly bound color–motion pairing, in which the central and peripheral regions share the same physical color–motion relationship, produces a stronger aftereffect than the misbinding condition ([Zhang et al., 2014](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/U28A); Figure S1). For this reason, the strength of a misbinding-induced CCMAE may be relatively weak to begin with.🔴

🔴A further consideration is that MAEs themselves do not always correspond to perceived motion: they can arise even when the adapting motion is not consciously perceived [(Maruya et al., 2008; Whitney & Bressler, 2007\)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/gICV+9tqT). This indicates that perceptual content and adaptation do not stand in a one-to-one relationship, a dissociation that may also hold for the CCMAE. Relatedly, color–motion misbinding may arise from higher-level perceptual inference processes that do not strongly modulate low-level visual representations. Several previous findings show the importance of higher-level perceptual inference for misbinding. [Wang & Shevell (2014)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/36Hc) reported that the illusion persists even when the peripheral colors differ slightly from the central colors. This suggests that color signals in the peripheral effect part are themselves unstable and ambiguous, allowing information from the central inducer part to influence the perceived color of peripheral elements. Further evidence comes from [Stepien & Shevell (2015)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/mO3P), who found that misbinding became more frequent when all dots were rendered achromatic. Removing color differences increases the similarity between central and peripheral elements, suggesting that the illusion depends on establishing a correspondence between central and peripheral regions. Thus, misbinding may reflect a process that resolves the ambiguity of peripheral information by relying on the feature binding firmly established in central vision, when pre-attentive features are similar across the entire visual field. These results are consistent with recent accounts in which the periphery, being more uncertain, inherits appearance from the fovea through extrapolation or filling-in from foveal information [(Stewart et al., 2020; Toscani et al., 2017\)](https://paperpile.com/c/PvgUEu/HuOH+a1Yn). We emphasize that our null PSE result does not itself establish this higher-level account: the account is an interpretive hypothesis grounded in prior literature, and our data are equally compatible with a low-level misbinding-induced aftereffect that the present design lacked the power, or the appropriate control condition, to detect with confidence (see above). Nor do we intend low-level adaptation and higher-level inference as mutually exclusive explanations: a perceptual process that resolves peripheral ambiguity by borrowing central feature bindings could still leave a residual, low-level adaptation signature that a more sensitive design might detect.🔴

🔴We cannot adjudicate between these two broad possibilities with the present data, and we offer the cancellation account above as a tentative conjecture rather than an established explanation. What can be said is that, whichever of these possibilities is correct, a misbinding-induced CCMAE is evidently not as robust as previously claimed. If the second possibility holds, the following broader interpretation may apply.🔴

🔴Wu et al.'s illusion has been labeled "misbinding", a term that implies a failure of feature binding that alters early sensory representations. In light of the considerations above, we suggest that this phenomenon may instead sit at the intersection of attentional feature binding and peripheral representation, drawing on higher-order integrative processes that construct a coherent visual experience across the entire visual field.🔴
